newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: BIS audited report to detail Nazi gold dealings.
newsitem.headline: BIS audited report to detail Nazi gold dealings.

text.p: The Bank for International Settlements (BIS), one of the most secretive international institutions, will on Monday release an audited report about its dealings with Nazi gold that is based on its archives, up to now hermetically sealed from public view.
The report is bound to disappoint those that expect its dusty archives to contain sensational revelations about its past because it largely confirms recent statements by BIS management.
"The report will show that the BIS dealt with German gold during the war, but it is clear that BIS was not the main outlet for Reichsbank gold," a banking source said.
BIS was created in 1930 to oversee German reparations to the Allied Powers after World War One and physically received 12 tonnes of gold from Germany's Reichsbank between 1939 and 1945.
This amount compares with a total of 336 tonnes of gold that was shipped from the Reichsbank to other countries, including the Swiss National Bank (SNB), during World War Two.
"The report will retrace all BIS' transactions with the Reichsbank, where the gold ended up, the purpose of the transaction and what it was used for," a BIS source said.

Although the report contains few new major historical facts, it is significant because it gives a foretaste of BIS' archives and sheds further light on Switzerland's role during World War Two, an issue under scrutiny.
BIS is also releasing the report to put an end to lingering speculation, suspicion and errors about its war-time role, a role that was heavily criticised during and after the war.

"Without the unvarnished story about the BIS, the history about Switzerland's financial dealings in World War Two remain incomplete," Swiss journalist and author Gian Trepp wrote in his book Banking With the Enemy, one of the most thorough accounts of BIS's dealings.
The report seeks to redress some of the errors that have crept into accounts about its dealings.
But past attempts to correct allegations about BIS' dealings have lacked credibility because its archives were sealed and it could neither prove or disprove any allegations.
The report is based on a detailed account that was sent to U.S. Senator Alfonse D'Amato last year.
D'Amato has spearheaded U.S. inquiries into dormant Jewish accounts in Switzerland and been a vocal critic of Swiss bank's handling of the sensitive issue.

BIS, the world's oldest international financial institution, has been preparing to open its archives to historians for the last two years and souces expect the archives to be opened to historians next year.

BIS management has already said that the Volcker Commission and the commision of historians that has been charged by the Swiss government to look into country's dealings with Nazi Germany are welcome to search its archives.
Of the 12 tonnes of gold that BIS received from the Reichsbank, around half was interest payments from Germany.
Under the Young Plan and the Hague Agreement, which established the BIS in 1930, BIS invested money in Germany and in return the Reichsbank paid interest to BIS.
The other half of the gold paid by Germany to BIS covered German debts in a European postal clearing system and payments to Yugoslav railways.
Until 1943 the Reichsbank mainly paid interest in currency, but after 1943 all interest was in the form of gold.

A total of 13.5 tonnes of gold was actually transferred by the Reichsbank to BIS accounts, but a final shipment of 1.5 tonnes in April 1945 never reached Switzerland because it was stopped at the German-Swiss border.
After World War Two, BIS handed back 3.7 tonnes of gold to the Allied Powers. The gold was identified as looted by the Germans from the central banks of the Netherlands and Belgium.
